tldr: This paper applies Evolution Strategies (ES), a black-box optimization approach, to continual control tasks for the first time. It demonstrates that a simple "replay" mechanism—mixing in evaluations from past tasks—significantly prevents catastrophic forgetting.
hero_caption: Conceptual diagram of Continual Evolution Strategies (Continual ES) in parameter space. Naively chasing single-task optima (marked with crosses) leads to forgetting previous knowledge. By introducing replay as a constraint, the optimization trajectory is guided toward a compromise region (open circle) that balances performance across multiple tasks.
overview:
In reinforcement learning and robot control, tasks and environments constantly change over time. However, when a standard neural network is sequentially trained on new tasks, it suffers from "catastrophic forgetting," completely wiping out previously learned behaviors. Most continual learning research to date has relied on gradient descent. As a result, very little was actually known about how Evolution Strategies (ES)—which explore black-box landscapes using populations—behave when tasks change sequentially.

To investigate this, the authors systematically studied the continual learning behavior of ES on sequential MuJoCo locomotion tasks (Hopper, Swimmer, and Walker2d). They found that vanilla ES over-adapts to new tasks and severely forgets past tasks when no countermeasures are taken.

To tackle this problem, the authors introduced "replay." During the population evaluation phase in ES, rollouts from previously experienced tasks are added alongside the current task and ranked together. Without any gradient computations or major network architecture changes, this enables the agent to acquire new motions while preserving past motor skills. Furthermore, the experiments revealed a stability-plasticity trade-off, where allocating too much replay budget reduces adaptation to new tasks (plasticity), as well as positive transfer of knowledge from legged robots to a swimming robot.
contributions: Providing the first comprehensive empirical evaluation applying Evolution Strategies (ES), a black-box optimization method, to continual control tasks.
Demonstrating that a simple replay mechanism—mixing in evaluation samples from past tasks and rank-normalizing them together—dramatically mitigates catastrophic forgetting in ES.
Quantifying the trade-off between the replay compute budget, past retention (stability), and new adaptation (plasticity) using an interference metric.
Uncovering the asymmetry of knowledge transfer across robot morphologies, demonstrating positive transfer where learning on legged robots facilitates adaptation to a swimming robot.

sections.heading: Toward Robots That Do Not Forget How to Move When Environments Change
sections.summary: Continual adaptation to environmental and morphological changes is essential in robot control, but prior continual learning research has heavily favored gradient-based methods. This study is the first to uncover how Evolution Strategies (ES), a prominent alternative to reinforcement learning, adapt and forget across sequential task transitions.
sections.details:
Current deep-learning-based controllers are generally optimized under the assumption that environmental dynamics and robot morphology remain constant. In real-world operation, however, operating environments fluctuate continuously: robots encounter unknown surfaces, or their payloads and actuator states change. Sequentially training conventional single-task optimization models on new tasks triggers catastrophic forgetting, overwriting previously acquired policies and rendering them useless.

Continual learning research so far has centered on gradient-based methods, such as supervised learning and policy gradients. On the other hand, Evolution Strategies (ES)—which explore via populations by perturbing policy parameters with noise—are known to excel in sparse-reward environments and non-differentiable control problems. Despite this, their behavior in streaming task environments has remained unexplored.

Crucially, because ES is a black-box optimizer that does not use gradients, existing gradient-constrained approaches cannot be applied directly. This study benchmarks the continual control performance of ES across sequences of MuJoCo locomotion tasks. It demonstrates that naive ES suffers from severe forgetting, and that incorporating proper re-evaluation of past tasks (replay) enables new adaptation while retaining past behaviors.

sections.heading: Tackling Continual Learning with Evolutionary Computation in a Gradient-Dominated Field
sections.summary: While replay methods that retain past memories are prominent in continual learning, combining them with evolutionary approaches has been limited to a few hybrid methods. This paper is distinctive in directly and quantitatively evaluating forgetting, transfer, and adaptation in continuous control tasks using pure ES.
sections.details:
The goal of continual learning is to continuously adapt to a stream of new tasks without destroying previously acquired knowledge. The most widely used countermeasure is "replay," which blends past data or experiences into current learning. In particular, the "task-agnostic" setting—where the robot is not given an ID (label) indicating which task it is currently executing—requires a single policy network to handle all tasks, posing an extremely difficult challenge.

Prior work using evolutionary computation for continual adaptation was limited to a few studies, such as CEM-ACER and ES-TD3 combining evolutionary search with Actor-Critic actor updates, or evolutionary continual learning applied to supervised learning like image classification. In robotics and continuous control, no prior study had thoroughly measured and analyzed the dynamics of forgetting, knowledge transfer, and adaptation interference using pure ES alone. This work leads the way in that domain.

sections.heading: A Natural Mechanism for Integrating Replay into Evolution Strategies
sections.summary: The authors established a protocol to learn sequentially without resetting parameters across tasks, introducing an "ES replay" mechanism that mixes evaluations from past tasks into the current search population. They defined Backward Transfer (BWT), Forward Transfer (FWT), and Interference at acquisition (Int) as metrics to measure continual learning success from multiple angles.
sections.details:
In this framework, a single policy parameter $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is sequentially optimized across an ordered sequence of tasks $\mathcal{T}=(T_1, \dots, T_n)$ without resetting. Three MuJoCo environments were chosen: Hopper-v5 (one-legged hopping), Walker2d-v5 (bipedal walking), and Swimmer-v5 (underwater swimming). Because their skeletal structures and control dynamics differ substantially, noticeable competition arises when learning them sequentially.

The policy network features task-specific input projection layers to accommodate differing observation dimensions across tasks, followed by shared hidden layers (64 ReLU units) and a shared output layer (action decision head). In the task-agnostic setting without explicit task IDs, the exact same output head must produce joint torques for all robots.

A standard parallel ES is used as the optimization algorithm. At each generation $t$, $\lambda$ candidate solutions $\theta_t + \sigma \varepsilon_i$ perturbed by Gaussian noise $\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ are executed in the environment to obtain returns $F_i$. Parameters are then updated using weights derived from rank-normalized rewards.

The key innovation lies in how replay is integrated. Why does replay fit ES so well? Because it requires no additional gradient calculations or complex sampling from replay buffers. When evaluating candidate solutions for the current task, the same perturbed parameters are also evaluated in environments of past tasks. Those rewards are gathered, rank-normalized together with current-task rewards, and reflected in the parameter update with equal weighting. This naturally steers the search center toward parameter regions that sustain high performance on past tasks as well.

Learning is evaluated using normalized rewards $\hat{R}$, scaled by baseline maximum rewards $R^*_{\mathrm{base}_i}$ obtained by training each task from scratch. In addition, the paper formulates Backward Transfer (BWT: negative values indicate forgetting, positive values indicate improvement), Forward Transfer (FWT: positive values indicate accelerated learning due to past experience), and Interference at acquisition ($\mathrm{Int}$: how much past memory hinders acquiring a new task) to evaluate performance.

sections.heading: Battling Forgetting: The Powerful Impact and Trade-offs of Replay
sections.summary: Naive ES suffered catastrophic forgetting, with past performance dropping nearly to zero immediately after task transitions. Moderate replay maintained past performance at a high level. Experiments also revealed a trade-off where too much replay hinders new task learning, along with asymmetric positive transfer from legged locomotion to swimming.
sections.details:
The experimental hyperparameters were set to population size $\lambda = 768 \pm 384$, perturbation noise standard deviation $\sigma = 0.1$, learning rate $\eta = 0.05$, and 1000 generations per task. Evaluations were conducted every 10 generations using unperturbed deterministic policies, recording averages over 10 rollouts.

- 4.1 Task-Agnostic Continual Learning (Limits of Naive ES):
When training without replay in the order Hopper $\to$ Swimmer $\to$ Walker2d, an astonishingly rapid catastrophic forgetting occurred (Figure F2). Immediately after completing Hopper training and beginning Swimmer training, the normalized reward for Hopper plummeted close to zero. Transitioning to Walker2d caused Swimmer performance to drop as well. This shows that without interventions, naive ES completely discards past control skills.

- 4.2 Mitigating Forgetting via Replay and the Associated Trade-off:
The authors examined replay's effects by varying replay perturbation steps across 12 (about 1.5%), 192 (about 25%), and 288 (about 37.5%). As shown in Figure F3 (+192 steps), rewards on Hopper and Swimmer remained at high levels even across task switches, while Walker2d was successfully learned. Replay successfully directed the search into parameter regions that accommodate multiple tasks.
However, more replay is not always better. Analyzing interference at new task acquisition ($\mathrm{Int}$) in Figure F4 reveals that without replay (0 steps), interference for Walker2d exceeds 0.7 due to past bias. Adding 192 steps of replay dramatically lowers interference. Yet increasing it to 288 steps causes interference to rise again. This reflects the stability-plasticity trade-off: excessive consideration for past tasks constrains the acquisition of new movements.

- 4.3 Knowledge Transfer Across Tasks:
Comprehensive testing across all six task permutations (Figure F5) showed that Backward Transfer (BWT) hovered near zero (preventing forgetting) for most sequences thanks to replay. Interestingly, Forward Transfer (FWT) displayed clear asymmetry. Sequences moving from legged robots to the swimming robot (Hopper $\to$ Swimmer and Walker2d $\to$ Swimmer) exhibited significant positive forward transfer (FWT > 0). Alternating leg movements likely aided the acquisition of undulating propulsion. Conversely, Swimmer $\to$ Hopper resulted in negative transfer, highlighting a strong directionality in morphological compatibility.

captions.F2: Learning curves in the task-agnostic setting without replay. The moment the task boundary (vertical dotted line) is crossed, rewards for Hopper (blue line)—which had learned to hop well—fall vertically, showing that catastrophic forgetting is severe in naive ES.
captions.F3: Learning curves with about 25% (+192 steps) replay. As tasks shift to Swimmer (orange line) and Walker2d (green line), previously learned Hopper performance remains stable, substantially suppressing forgetting.
captions.F4: Interference at new task acquisition across different replay budgets. Interference during Walker2d learning is high with zero (0) or minimal (12) replay, and reaches its minimum at 192 steps. Increasing to 288 steps worsens interference due to excessive constraints, illustrating the trade-off.
captions.F5: Average Backward Transfer (BWT, left) and Forward Transfer (FWT, right) per task pair. BWT stays close to zero, showing forgetting is prevented. On the right, FWT is distinctly positive only for transfers from legged robots to Swimmer (H→S, W→S), demonstrating strong transfer asymmetry.

sections.heading: Can Evolution Strategies Become a Viable Contender for Continual Control?
sections.summary: Although ES suffers from interference issues similar to gradient methods, replay integrates into it very naturally. Future work points toward extending other continual learning approaches—such as model distillation and parameter-importance regularization—from gradient descent to black-box evolutionary methods.
sections.details:
As the experimental results demonstrate, Evolution Strategies experience catastrophic interference just like gradient-based methods. However, introducing a replay mechanism proves that ES can function effectively as a continual robot control framework. The primary strength of replay in ES lies in its implementation simplicity: it requires no loss function redesign or backpropagation computation graph, needing only a few extra rollouts of past tasks in the environment evaluation loop.

On the other hand, the study also revealed that cross-task knowledge transfer does not happen unconditionally; it depends heavily on morphological compatibility and task ordering. For future directions, the authors suggest importing and adapting continual learning concepts that have succeeded in gradient-based methods—such as knowledge distillation and synaptic plasticity-based importance weighting (e.g., EWC)—into black-box evolutionary optimization.

sections.heading: Appendix: Identifying the Root Cause of Interference via Task-Aware Heads
sections.summary: Testing a "task-aware" setup (separating output layers by task), where the robot knows its task ID, dramatically reduced forgetting. This confirms that the primary driver of interference in continual control is action semantic conflict in the shared output layer.
sections.details:
In the paper's appendices (Appendices B–D), detailed experiments examine a "Task-Aware" (multi-head) setting as a comparison to the primary "task-agnostic" (single shared output head) setup. In the task-aware setting, both input projection layers and output heads are dedicated to specific tasks, while only the intermediate layers (64-unit hidden layers) are shared across all tasks.

Figure F8 shows that simply separating output heads dramatically mitigates Hopper's performance decline after task switches, even without replay. Furthermore, comparing acquisition interference between the shared head with replay and task-specific heads in Figure F9 indicates that task-specific heads reduce interference across almost all task permutations.

This finding provides a clear insight: when continuously training robots with different morphologies, the primary bottleneck is not feature extraction (representations in hidden layers), but rather output-layer conflict caused by forcing different joint torque controls onto the exact same output units. This insight is highly relevant for designing continual learning systems on real-world robots.

takeaways: Applying naive Evolution Strategies (ES) directly to continual control causes catastrophic forgetting, but simple replay mixing in past task evaluations dramatically improves retention.
Increasing the replay budget indefinitely is counterproductive; excessive replay harms plasticity (new adaptation), making an appropriate allocation around 25% crucial.

Knowledge transfer across different robot morphologies exhibits strong asymmetry, with positive forward transfer occurring predominantly from legged locomotion (Hopper/Walker2d) to swimming (Swimmer).
The primary source of interference lies in the shared output layer; separating output heads per task (task-aware setup) avoids most forgetting on its own.
limitations: Evaluations are limited to three relatively simple 2D MuJoCo locomotion tasks (Hopper, Walker2d, and Swimmer).
Replay requires maintaining past simulator environments and executing additional rollouts, leaving sampling cost challenges for direct application to physical robots.
Pairs exhibiting positive forward transfer were extremely limited, indicating that further architectural innovations are needed to reliably harness general pre-training effects.
